analysis.one_liner: Repeals enhanced federal oversight of the largest nonbank financial firms, including major insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first day: introduced January 7, 2015, referred to the Senate Banking Committee with no cosponsors, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law that lets regulators designate big nonbank financial companies — such as insurers and other giants outside the traditional banking system — for tougher Federal Reserve oversight, including stricter capital requirements and stress-related standards. It would also repeal a law giving the Fed risk-management oversight over payment, clearing, and settlement systems, and eliminate required reports on how these firms would wind themselves down if they failed. Nothing in the bill replaces this oversight with another mechanism.
analysis.who_benefits: Large nonbank financial companies — insurers, asset managers, and other giants that Dodd-Frank subjected to Federal Reserve supervision — would be freed from heightened capital standards, reporting requirements, and resolution-planning mandates. Payment and clearing utilities would also escape Fed risk-management standards.

how_it_helps.text: Removes all Federal Reserve supervision of domestic and foreign nonbank financial companies, including heightened standards, safeguards, and minimum leverage capital requirements

Eliminates the Financial Stability Oversight Council's duty to identify systemically important financial market utilities and repeals its authority to require reports and resolution plans from nonbank financial companies
Repeals the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act of 2010, ending Fed risk-management oversight of payment and settlement systems
Removes reporting requirements and studies on resolving failing financial companies

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the residual risk: if a large insurer or other nonbank firm that had been stripped of consolidated oversight ran into trouble, there would be no required resolution plan or heightened capital cushion, and taxpayers could again be exposed to losses in a crisis, as happened in 2008.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals minimum leverage capital requirements and heightened prudential standards for nonbank financial companies without substituting any alternative oversight or resolution regime
It eliminates required plans for rapid and orderly resolution of firms in material financial distress, removing a safeguard designed to let big firms fail without taxpayer bailouts
It ends Fed risk-management supervision of payment, clearing, and settlement utilities, which handle the plumbing of everyday financial transactions

A supporter's honest cost: Dodd-Frank oversight is burdensome, and designation can carry implicit government backing — but repealing it outright leaves no tool for seeing trouble building at giant nonbank firms until a crisis is underway

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The sponsor framed the bill as stopping the expansion of too-big-to-fail, on the theory that tagging firms as systemically important cements their privileged status. Whatever the merit of that argument, the bill as written simply deletes the oversight with nothing in its place: the largest nonbank firms would escape capital, stress, reporting, and resolution-planning requirements while the risk of their failure would shift to the financial system and, ultimately, taxpayers. The costs fall on the public; the benefits fall on a handful of very large firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and died there — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter (R-LA) introduced S. 107 on January 7, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
The bill's only action after referral was none: the record shows no further committee or floor action for the remainder of the Congress

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and the broader financial system kept Dodd-Frank's enhanced oversight of big nonbank firms intact; the large financial companies that would have been freed from it did not get the repeal they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept Dodd-Frank oversight intact

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on January 7, 2015

against.name: Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after referral on January 7, 2015

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party, so its support never took a partisan shape.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (designated insurers, asset managers, and similar firms)
industries.note: These firms — companies like MetLife, Prudential, and AIG that Dodd-Frank subjected to Federal Reserve supervision — would shed heightened capital standards, stress-related standards, reporting duties, and required wind-down plans. Their gain comes at the public's cost, since taxpayers and the wider economy would absorb the risk if one of them failed without a resolution plan or capital cushion.

Repealing the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act frees these systems from Fed risk-management standards. Because they process the transactions ordinary people and businesses rely on, their reduced oversight raises systemwide risk.

The bill leaves bank holding companies under Federal Reserve supervision while freeing their nonbank competitors from comparable oversight, which would put regulated banks at a competitive disadvantage and could push activity toward the unregulated firms.
